title: The Sultan Who Fared Forth in the Habit of a Darwaysh (తెలుగు)

keywords: the sultan who fared forth in the habit of a darwaysh
full_text:
Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna, feeling that his courtiers shielded him from the realities of his realm, laid aside his embroidered robes, dressed in the patched wool cloak of a wandering dervish, and took up a beggar's bowl.

He walked out into the countryside, sleeping in modest caravanserais, sharing dry crusts with camel drivers, and listening to weavers and field workers.

In a remote village, he encountered an elderly farmer working late into the evening by candlelight. Mahmud asked: 'Venerable uncle, why dost thou toil when other men rest?'
The old man sighed: 'The local tax collector charges double taxes, threatening to confiscate my small olive grove. I must work day and night to pay his unlawful exactions, for our Sultan sits far away in his palace, unaware of our plight.'

Mahmud made careful notes in his memory. Moving to another town, he met a widow whose house had been seized by an unjust magistrate who altered the property deeds. She wept: 'If only Sultan Mahmud could hear my voice, he would restore my roof!'

For three weeks, Mahmud traveled as a dervish, gathering evidence of extortion, injustice, and hidden virtue.

Returning to Ghazna, the Sultan summoned a grand public audience. He ordered the corrupt tax collector and the dishonest magistrate to stand before the throne.
Stepping down from the dais, Mahmud cast aside his royal mantle to reveal the patched dervish cloak underneath!

The oppressors turned white as linen.
'Did you believe,' declared Mahmud, 'that because the Sultan was absent from his throne, heaven had closed its ears? I was the dervish who asked for water at your door; I saw the tears of the widow and the toil of the farmer.'

The Sultan immediately dismissed the corrupt officials, returned the confiscated lands, compensated the victims threefold from the royal treasury, and established a traveling court of justice. He proved that a king who walks with the humble rules with the eternal strength of truth.
moral: True majesty is found not in diadems and thrones, but in listening to the heartfelt sorrows of the humble. [TE]
